subject: Biology
title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
summary: Plant tissues are meristematic (dividing) or permanent (simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; complex: xylem and phloem).
Tissues are organised into three tissue systems: epidermal, ground (fundamental) and vascular.
Internal structure differs between dicot and monocot roots, stems and leaves — the number and arrangement of vascular bundles is the key.
Secondary growth (vascular cambium and cork cambium) increases girth in dicots and gymnosperms, giving annual rings, heartwood, sapwood and bark.

formulas.name: Meristems
formulas.formula: apical (root and shoot tips — length);  intercalary (base of internodes in grasses — regrowth after grazing);  lateral (vascular cambium, cork cambium — girth)

formulas.name: Simple permanent tissues
formulas.formula: parenchyma (thin walls, storage, photosynthesis);  collenchyma (corners thickened with cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin — mechanical support in young dicot stems);  sclerenchyma (lignified, dead — fibres and sclereids)

formulas.name: Xylem elements
formulas.formula: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres (dead);  xylem parenchyma (only living part)
formulas.note: Gymnosperms lack vessels (except Gnetum); angiosperms have vessels.

formulas.name: Phloem elements
formulas.formula: sieve tubes + companion cells (angiosperms), phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres (only dead part)
formulas.note: Gymnosperms have albuminous cells and sieve cells instead of sieve tubes and companion cells.

formulas.name: Protoxylem position
formulas.formula: exarch (protoxylem towards periphery — roots);  endarch (protoxylem towards centre — stems)

formulas.name: Vascular bundles
formulas.formula: radial (xylem and phloem on different radii — roots);  conjoint collateral open (with cambium — dicot stem);  conjoint closed (no cambium — monocot stem and leaves)

formulas.name: Dicot vs monocot root
formulas.formula: dicot: 2–4 xylem bundles (diarch–tetrarch), small pith, secondary growth;  monocot: more than 6 (polyarch), large pith, no secondary growth

formulas.name: Dicot vs monocot stem
formulas.formula: dicot: vascular bundles in a ring, open, endodermis (starch sheath), hypodermis collenchyma;  monocot: scattered bundles, closed, sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, water-containing cavities, hypodermis sclerenchyma, no pith/cortex distinction

formulas.name: Dorsiventral vs isobilateral leaf
formulas.formula: dicot: palisade + spongy mesophyll, more stomata on lower surface;  monocot: undifferentiated mesophyll, stomata equal on both surfaces, bulliform cells
formulas.note: Bulliform cells lose water and make grass leaves curl to reduce water loss.

formulas.name: Stomata
formulas.formula: dicot: bean-shaped guard cells;  grasses: dumb-bell-shaped guard cells;  stomatal apparatus = pore + guard cells + subsidiary cells

formulas.name: Secondary growth outputs
formulas.formula: vascular cambium → secondary xylem (inside) + secondary phloem (outside);  cork cambium (phellogen) → cork (phellem, outside) + secondary cortex (phelloderm, inside)

formulas.name: Periderm and bark
formulas.formula: periderm = phellem + phellogen + phelloderm;  bark = all tissues outside the vascular cambium (including secondary phloem)

formulas.name: Annual rings
formulas.formula: spring/early wood: lighter, wide vessels;  autumn/late wood: darker, narrow vessels;  one light + one dark band = one year
formulas.when: Dendrochronology (estimating the age of a tree).

examples.title: Root or stem section?
examples.problem: A section shows radial bundles with exarch xylem and a pericycle. Root or stem?
examples.solution: Root — radial bundles and exarch protoxylem are root features (stems have conjoint bundles with endarch protoxylem).

examples.title: Monocot stem
examples.problem: List three features that identify a monocot stem in a T.S.
examples.solution: Scattered vascular bundles, each with a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; bundles conjoint and closed; peripheral bundles smaller than central ones; water-containing cavities; no clear pith.

examples.title: Heartwood vs sapwood
examples.problem: Which part of an old trunk conducts water?
examples.solution: Sapwood (alburnum) — the outer, light-coloured secondary xylem. Heartwood (duramen) is dark, filled with tannins, resins, oils and gums, and is non-conducting but strong.

examples.title: Living cells in xylem
examples.problem: Which element of xylem is alive?
examples.solution: Xylem parenchyma. Tracheids, vessels and xylem fibres are dead at maturity.

examples.title: Bark components
examples.problem: Is secondary phloem a part of the bark?
examples.solution: Yes. Bark includes every tissue outside the vascular cambium: secondary phloem, phelloderm, phellogen and phellem.

examples.title: Grass leaf curling
examples.problem: Why do grass leaves roll up on a hot dry day?
examples.solution: Bulliform cells on the upper epidermis lose turgor and shrink, making the leaf roll inwards and reducing exposed surface and water loss.

topics.title: Epidermal tissue system
topics.explain: Epidermis (usually single layer, covered by a waxy cuticle — absent in roots), stomata, and appendages: root hairs (unicellular extensions of epidermal cells) and trichomes on stems (usually multicellular, branched or unbranched, may be secretory).

topics.title: Ground tissue system
topics.explain: All tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles: cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays in stems and roots; mesophyll in leaves.

topics.title: Endodermis and Casparian strips
topics.explain: The innermost cortical layer of roots; its cells have Casparian strips of water-impermeable suberin on radial and inner tangential walls, forcing water to pass through living cells.

topics.title: Formation of the cambial ring
topics.explain: In dicot stems, intrafascicular cambium (within bundles) joins with interfascicular cambium (from medullary ray cells) to form a complete ring. Cambium is more active on the inner side, so more secondary xylem than phloem forms.

topics.title: Lenticels
topics.explain: Lens-shaped openings in the bark where phellogen forms loosely packed complementary cells instead of cork; they permit gas exchange between the outer atmosphere and inner tissues.

topics.title: Secondary growth in roots
topics.explain: The vascular cambium in dicot roots arises partly from conjunctive tissue below the phloem and partly from the pericycle opposite the protoxylem, forming a wavy ring that later becomes circular.

ratta: Xylem: only parenchyma living;  phloem: only fibres dead.
Root: radial, exarch;  stem: conjoint, endarch.
Dicot root 2–4 bundles; monocot root more than 6.
Dicot stem: ring, open;  monocot stem: scattered, closed.
